title: The lote tree of the boundary
hookLine: he saw Jibril at the lote tree of the utmost boundary, near the garden (53:13–15)
last: YOU KNOW BETTER THE AFFAIRS OF YOUR WORLD.

lines: THE SIDR: A HARDY DESERT TREE.
WATER AND SIDR FOR WASHING THE DEAD.
ONE AT THE EDGE OF CREATION.
cards: Sidr is a thorny tree of the Arabian desert, the lote tree: small leaves, small fruit, shade in a hard place.
In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells the women washing his daughter's body to use water and sidr, a practice that continues at funerals today. An ordinary desert tree.
And the Qur'an puts one at the edge of everything, at a boundary commentators describe as the farthest point anything created can reach.

teach.b: Surah An-Najm describes two times the Prophet saw the angel Jibril in his true form. The first was on the horizon, near the beginning.
The second, in Pickthall's translation: "And verily he saw him yet another time By the lote-tree of the utmost boundary, Nigh unto which is the Garden of Abode."
Sidrat al-muntaha. Muntaha means the end point, the furthest limit. Commentators explain it as the place beyond which no created being passes, where the knowledge of creatures stops.

They link this second sighting to the Night Journey and Ascension, the Isra' and Mi'raj, when the Prophet was taken through the heavens. 'A'ishah and Ibn Mas'ud both said, in reports in the two Sahihs, that what he saw at the tree was Jibril as he truly is; Ibn Mas'ud reported six hundred wings.

teach.h: FRUIT LIKE JARS, LEAVES LIKE EARS.
teach.b: The hadith of the Ascension in Bukhari describes the tree itself: fruits like great clay jars, leaves like elephants' ears, rivers flowing from its roots.
Then something covered the tree, a covering the surah doesn't name, and commentators call it beyond description.
And a short line: the sight did not swerve, nor did it go beyond. At the edge of everything, he didn't look away, and he didn't grab for more than he was shown. Notice the image.
Not a palace or a throne at the boundary, but a tree, the kind that gives shade in hard places.

how: Muslims remember the Isra' and Mi'raj, some with a yearly observance in the month of Rajab, retelling the journey to the lote tree and the gift of the five daily prayers; sidr leaves are still used in many places for washing the dead.

o: the end point, the farthest limit of creation
the city where the Night Journey began
a tall tree that grows only in paradise

games.q: the lote tree — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an describes in detail what covered the tree
it says something covered it and doesn't name it; commentators call it beyond description.
the lote tree is an ordinary desert tree in Arabia
the sidr, hardy and shade-giving, its leaves used to wash the dead.
commentators link the second sighting to the Night Journey and Ascension

games.q: you stand at the farthest boundary of creation and something indescribable covers the tree. what does the surah say the Prophet's sight did?
o: it reached for more than it was shown.
it did not swerve, nor go beyond.
games.why: 53:17: steady, without looking away and without overreaching.

practice: Sit at an edge, a doorstep, a window, the end of a street, or picture one, with inside on one side and outside on the other.
Look steadily at what's in front of you, the way the verse describes: without swerving, and without reaching for more. If you pray, ask for that steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Muntaha: the end point, the furthest limit any created being can reach, marked by the lote tree where the Prophet saw Jibril again. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the lote tree of the utmost boundary (53:14).

carryVoice: Your line: the farthest tree. The edge of everything is marked by something that gives shade. Good to see you today.
